content.content:
usage: facts-extract.sh [--check] [--part N] [--page-bytes N] [--root DIR] [--common] [QUERY ...]

Prints what the queries name, whole and in the order they are given; a rung's
briefing is one such command. Each piece comes under a line naming its file
and section. The output comes in parts of at most PAGE_BYTES (default 28000);
part 1 opens with the size of the whole output in bytes and estimated tokens,
then what was asked for, where it is and what was not found; each part says
whether there is a next one, and --part N prints part N.

QUERY is one of:
  TITLE                  the FACTS.md entry whose title holds TITLE: an entry's
                         title is its bold opening, or where it has none, its
                         opening words up to the first colon, semicolon or full stop
  section:HEADING        every entry of the FACTS.md section whose heading holds HEADING
  index:WORDS            the INDEX.md lines that hold every one of WORDS (at most 10)
  ledger:ROW             row ROW of the gap ledger, whole, under its section and
                         the table's header
  positions:DATE WORDS   the entry of POSITIONS.md dated DATE (YYYY-MM-DD, the first
                         date in the entry) whose head, the entry's text up to its
                         first colon and space, holds every one of WORDS; when no
                         entry of POSITIONS.md matches, the entry of
                         POSITIONS-history.md, with the line saying what became of
                         it; the output says which file it came from
  map:FILE#HEADING       the section of explorations/coordinator/map/FILE whose
                         heading holds HEADING, down to the next heading of its level
  doc:PATH#HEADING       the same for any note, PATH from the repository root, such
                         as a judge's ruling; doc:PATH alone prints the whole note;
                         in a .tex or .tick file the headings are its \chapter, \section,
                         \subsection, \subsubsection and \paragraph titles,
                         matched with their macros dropped; a heading equal to
                         HEADING wins over the headings that merely hold it, and
                         HEADING may be a path, A > B, for B's section inside A's
  map:FILE#HEADING@WORDS, doc:PATH#HEADING@WORDS
                         only the table rows and list items of that section that
                         hold every one of WORDS, a row under its table's header,
                         and the paragraphs whose bold lead holds them
  code:PATH#FROM         the declaration that starts on the one line of PATH that
                         holds FROM, with its line numbers: in .java, .scala and
                         .js through the brace that closes it, elsewhere (.fss,
                         .fsi) through its more indented lines and its end
  code:PATH#FROM..TO     from the declaration at FROM through the end of the
                         one at the first line after it that holds TO
WORDS match as whole words, or as the start of one when a word ends in *.
Matching ignores case, backticks and double quotes, reads curly quotes as
straight ones, and takes any run of spaces as one space.

  --check             print one line per query, what it matches, where, and its
                      size in bytes, then the size of the whole output, and
                      nothing else; exit 1 unless every query matches exactly
                      one place (an index topic: at least one line)
  --part N            print part N of the output (default 1)
  --page-bytes N      the size of a part (default 28000)
  --root DIR          read the record and every map: and doc: path from the
                      checkout at DIR instead of this tool's own
  --common            first print the record's shared sections: the map's
                      README "Terms used here", "The shape of the system" and
                      "Touch this, and that moves", PLAN.md's "The phases", and
                      explorations/repo-internals.md whole; no role of the batch
                      script reads them whole, and a planner reads them to
                      choose a rung's slices

## 2. Static and dynamic agreement

**Verdict.** For the question's call, it holds on the compiled path. Walk needs a rule written: dispatch again on the converted values. The two paths still differ where a static type is wider than its value, as they do for every promoted call under batch N.

- **The option-2 call itself.** Written out as `op[\ZZ64\](z, w)`, or inferred by opt2 as `op(z, w)`: the compiled run prints `op generic[ ZZ64 , ZZ64 ]` (`captures/O2Explicit.*`). The run-time dispatch keeps the generic instance, since the arm over `Any` is less specific.
- **A more specific arm that fits the converted values runs.** Take the generic arm beside `op(a: ZZ64, b: ZZ64)` (`O2Z64`). The rule and opt2 both choose the generic arm at `ZZ64` statically (by reading `rule.patch`: the plain arm needs a coercion, so it is not in the first attempt, which holds only the promoted generic). The compiled run then prints `op plain64[ ZZ64 , ZZ64 ]` for `op(z, w)`, and so does the written-out `op[\ZZ64\](z, w)` on the stock build (`O2Z64Rest.stock.txt`). The generic instance's own class tests the more specific arms first; the stock stack shows it (`op⟦Union⟦FZZ32,FZZ64⟧⟧.the_function`, check 7). This is the specification's dynamic rule: the declarations applicable at run time are considered (`basic/overloading.tex:262-276`), and the dynamic choice is more specific than the static one (`advanced/overloading.tex:466-468`; the implementation strategy at `:72-77`). The return-type rule over every instance keeps it type-safe (answer 9). So under option 2, walk must do the same: after K's inference converts, dispatch on the converted values. That rule has to be written for rungs K and W. Walk refuses this set at load today, in both modes ("at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types", `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:527`; `captures/O2Z64.walk-*.txt`), so walk's side could not be measured.
- **A static type wider than the value.** The brief's "static type narrower than its run-time type" cannot occur under a sound checker. The measured shape is the other way round: `n: Number` holding a `ZZ32` (`O2Wide`).
  - Compiled, on stock, rule and opt2: `op(n, w)` runs the generic arm at `T = Number`, unconverted, `generic[ ZZ32 , ZZ64 ]`.
  - Walk sees only run-time types. Stock gives `generic[ZZ32,ZZ64]` (the join). Apply, which is option 1 as probe K built it, gives `plain[ZZ32,ZZ64]`: the paths disagree on the arm. Under option 2, walk would choose the generic arm and K's rule would convert: `generic[ZZ64,ZZ64]`. That is by reading, from the two measured halves (walk stock's choice here; apply's conversion in `same(z, w)`). The arm then agrees and the instance differs.
  - The same instance split exists with no plain arm at all: `same(n, w)` prints `[ ZZ32 , ZZ64 ]` compiled and `[ZZ64,ZZ64]` under walk apply (`O2Lone`). So the split is rung K's (walk promotes from run-time types, where the specification resolves coercion statically, `conversions-coercions.tex:584-591`), not option 2's. Option 2 turns option 1's split on the arm into that split on the instance.
- **Arguments typed `Any`.** `op(a, aw)` with a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` inside (`O2Lone`).
  - Compiled, on all three builds: `plain[ ZZ32 , ZZ64 ]`. The dispatcher joins two run-time types only when one is a supertype of the other (javap: two `runtimeSupertypeOf` tests, then the plain arm, `captures/javap-O2Explicit.txt`; `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/OverloadSet.java:1609`, "fails if cannot join w/o union"). With two `ZZ32`s it does reach the generic arm: `op(a, a2)` prints `generic[ ZZ32 , ZZ32 ]`.
  - Walk: stock `generic[ZZ32,ZZ64]`, apply `plain`, and option 2 `generic[ZZ64,ZZ64]` by reading.
  - So option 2 keeps today's split on this shape, and option 1 closes it. By reading, the specification's own answer is the generic arm at the join, unconverted, since coercion is resolved statically and a run-time choice converts nothing (`conversions-coercions.tex:584-591`). That is walk stock's answer. No build gives it under batch N, whichever option is taken.
- **The arms in the other order.** `O2Rev` (the plain arm first) gives the same answers as the unreversed pair on every build and in both walk modes. Walk's dependence on declaration order (defect 1, `overloading-judgement.md:113`) arises between a generic instance and a plain arm with equal domains: the `O2Z64` shape, which walk refuses at load today.

## 5. Numerals and rung Q

**Verdict.** Reading A holds. Reading B needs an exact rule for which conversions go uncounted.

- **Measured on the compiled path** (`O2Num`), whose numeral is already the sibling `IntLiteral` of the numeral switch (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:390`):
  - the rule (option 1): `op(1, w)` gives `plain[ IntLiteral , ZZ64 ]`, `op(1, z)` gives `plain[ IntLiteral , ZZ32 ]`, `op(1, 2)` gives `generic[ IntLiteral , IntLiteral ]`;
  - opt2: `op(1, w)` gives `generic[ ZZ64 , ZZ64 ]`, `op(1, z)` gives `generic[ ZZ32 , ZZ32 ]`, `op(1, 2)` gives `generic[ IntLiteral , IntLiteral ]`.
- **Reading A.** `IntLiteral` extends `Number`, so `(IntLiteral, ZZ64)` lies in the generic arm's declared domain. The generic arm is chosen, and `T = ZZ64` converts the numeral. That is what answer 8 says of integer literals, and what the shadow gives a lone `same(3, w)` (`inference-rule-shadow.md:57`). For `op(1, 2)`, `T = IntLiteral` under both options. The bound is met, so Q1's default (`ZZ32` when a numeral's own type does not meet the bound, `CLIMB-BATCH-N.md:96`) never arises.
- **Row 79 and rung Q's test.** `ee(5)`, with `ee[\nat n\](x: ZZ32)` beside `ee(x: Any)`, must take the arm applicable without coercion (rung Q's test, `CLIMB-BATCH-N.md`, section Q). It prints 2 on stock, rule and opt2 (`O2Pos`). Reading A agrees: `ee`'s declared domain is `ZZ32`, and a numeral is not in it.
- **The exemption must be exact.** opt2 exempts every coercion of a generic candidate, and one shape flips. `gg[\T extends Number\](x: ZZ32, y: T)` beside `gg(x: Any, y: Any)`: `gg(5, w)` prints `plain[ IntLiteral , ZZ64 ]` on stock and rule, and `generic[ ZZ32 , ZZ64 ]` on opt2 (`O2Pos`). That converts a numeral at a declared `ZZ32` parameter although the arm over `Any` takes it as it is, which the coercion order forbids. Reading A has no exemption to get wrong: `gg`'s declared domain holds no `IntLiteral` in position 1. A reading-B rule would have to name exactly the conversions it leaves uncounted: only those at a parameter whose declared type is a lone type parameter that the promotion chooses. That excludes a declared type (row 388's `gf`) and a type parameter fixed elsewhere (a lifted `T` fixed by the receiver, as in question B's `w MAX z`, `before-n-questions.md:51`).
- **Walk.** Before the switch, walk's numeral is a `ZZ32`, so its `O2Num` rows are the `z` rows. After rung Q, by reading, walk behaves as the compiled path does.

component OpAnyZW
export Executable
(* The legal form of probe K's fork: the plain arm over a strict supertype of the generic arm's
   domain, so the pair passes the No Duplicates rule the checker enforces (OpZW.stock.txt). *)
op[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T): String = "op generic[" (typeOf a) "," (typeOf b) "]"
op(a: Any, b: Any): String = "op plain[" (typeOf a) "," (typeOf b) "]"
typeOf(x: Any): String = typecase x of

    ZZ64 => "ZZ64"
    else => "other"
  end

Batch N is the inference rule with the numeral switch, which you agreed at 19:30 UTC on 2026-09-27: the compiled checker infers a generic's type arguments with coercion and keeps the expected type at a call written `f(x)`, walk does the same when it dispatches, a numeral gets a type of its own that each number type converts from, and the specification's empty type-inference chapter is written. Since 19:06 UTC on 2026-09-28 it also carries the two decisions of the conversion judgement you accepted, the rule for which declaration runs when conversions meet overloading and row 484's library fix, and since 19:17 UTC your answer to item 25, a size used as a value converting to `ZZ32` as a numeral does. It runs after batches 7R and 7C and batch 6.5's first run, and before batch 7b. A rung is one fix, built test-first by one worker in its own copy of the tree and judged by a second worker, the skeptic, before the batch is merged and the whole test suite (the gate) runs once.

In plain words: when a program calls a generic function without writing its type arguments, the checker works them out from the arguments. Today it uses only subtyping, so `scale(b, 3)` for a box of `RR64` is refused although `3` converts to `RR64`, and a `ZZ32` beside a `ZZ64` gives a union type instead of `ZZ64`. Walk makes the same mistakes at run time. And a numeral such as `3` is typed three ways today: the compiled checker calls it `IntLiteral`, the one library declares that `IntLiteral` below `ZZ32`, and walk makes it a `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ` by its size. This batch makes both paths infer with coercion, then gives the numeral its own type. Where a call could be served by more than one declaration, a conversion is used only to make the call possible, never to change which declaration runs when one already fits; a generic declaration that fits is then instantiated at the narrowest type every argument converts into, as your answer 8 says.

opr =(a:Any, b:Any):Boolean = a SEQV b
    (** Two exact numbers of different types compare as rationals; a float
        compares with any number after %asFloat%, so an exact value equals
        its nearest float. **)
    opr =(self, other:Number):Boolean =
        typecase self of
            RR64 => (asFloat(self) = asFloat(other))
            else => typecase other of
                        RR64 => (asFloat(self) = asFloat(other))
                        else => (exactValue(self) = exactValue(other))
                    end
        end
end

exactValue(x: Number): QQ =
    typecase x of
        q: QQ => q
        z: ZZ32 => do q: QQ = z; q end
        z: ZZ64 => do q: QQ = z; q end
        z: NN32 => do q: QQ = z; q end
        z: NN64 => do q: QQ = z; q end
        z: ZZ => do q: QQ = z; q end
        else => Ratio(0, 0)
    end

                for l in lines:
                    if verbose or 'NOT FOUND' in l or 'not one' in l or 'entries' in l: print('   ', l[:300])
            if r.returncode: bad += 1
    print('bad lists', bad)
    sys.exit(1 if bad else 0)
